svg.title: A chart for vCenter administrators that picks the way to give someone access to a VKS cluster. Find the row that fits. 1: a tool or a person that must be able to do everything in the cluster gets an administrator token. 2: a pipeline, a tool or a team sharing one login in one namespace gets a ServiceAccount token. 3: a person with a vCenter SSO account uses their own account. 4: people in an identity provider registered on the Supervisor use their group through the Supervisor. 5: people in a provider that is not registered use the provider on one new cluster (a dashed row). 6: one person with no SSO or identity provider account, for a limited time, gets a personal certificate; deleting its binding stops its rights, but the certificate itself cannot be withdrawn. 7: never send the cluster's built-in administrator file; send the row 1 token only if they need everything. Each row shows who sets it up, what the person installs, how long it lasts, how it is taken away and what you send. A band at the top warns that Can edit or Owner on the vSphere Namespace makes someone administrator of every VKS cluster in it and lets them download the file you never send; rows 3 and 4 need a role from you, row 5 a new cluster. A strip explains one namespace versus the whole cluster; read-only access is one namespace at a time. Footnotes and a legend explain how each way is taken away.

text.tspan: Which way in? Access to a VKS cluster
Find the row that fits your customer. Each way has its own login, so you never send the cluster's administrator file and can take each
Your step in vCenter: the role on the vSphere Namespace
They may sign in; no rights inside the cluster until

can download the file you never send
Rows 3 and 4 need a role from you for your customer; row 5 needs a new cluster, made by someone with Namespaces Edit (Can edit); rows 1, 2 and 6 are made

One team namespace inside the cluster (not
the vSphere Namespace): the normal choice
"*": cluster-admin on the whole cluster; the
Left empty: the step stops and changes
Rows 2, 4 and 6 can take "*": row 2 for a whole-cluster login that must end after DAYS, row 4 for a group with Can view, row 6 for a person who must administer the
cluster; rows 3 and 5 refuse it. For lasting whole-cluster access the guides send row 1, which can be taken away. Read only: row 2 or 4 with view, one namespace
each; there is no read-only whole-cluster way.
(1) Tokens and workloads made with edit keep running: delete the workloads, re-create the ServiceAccounts with rights and restart what uses them; never give edit
where software with wider rights runs. Disabling a person's SSO or identity-provider account does not stop a ServiceAccount token.
(2) With whole-cluster rights the holder can make other logins of their own; after a leak, only a new cluster is certain to be clean.
(3) Taking it away removes its name's rights; the certificate still proves that name until its end date, so never give that name rights again.
(4) One person on row 4: disable them or end their sessions, not only remove them from a group.
(5) Never forward a person's own login file: it acts as them.
